summary: An early Telnet option, written in 1974, that lets two sides negotiate how a remote system handles horizontal tab stops on output. It is one of a family of small options by the same author covering how a terminal's output formatting is handled. It is historic and no longer used in practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This Telnet option lets the data sender and receiver agree who handles horizontal tab stops and which columns are stops. It also defines what happens when the parties do not agree to negotiate.

subtitle: A Telnet option for negotiating who handles horizontal tab stops and where they are placed.

tldr.problem: A sender and receiver need to coordinate which side handles horizontal tab stops and what positions to use.
tldr.mechanism: The NAOHTS option lets either party negotiate responsibility and exchange tab-stop column numbers through subnegotiation.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines default behavior and rules for deciding which party handles tab stops when one or both parties volunteer.

today: RFC 653 is Historic according to the unit metadata. It documents the NAOHTS Telnet option and its negotiation rules.

sections.title: The NAOHTS Option
sections.content:
RFC 653 defines NAOHTS, short for Negotiate About Output Horizontal Tabstops. The option applies to a simplex connection and lets the data sender and receiver negotiate which party handles horizontal tab-stop processing.

Without further subnegotiation after agreement, the data receiver is assumed to handle output tab stops.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is about which side of a Telnet connection handles horizontal tab stops. By default after agreement, the receiver handles them.

sections.title: Negotiating Tab-Stop Responsibility
sections.content:
IAC DO NAOHTS and IAC WILL NAOHTS request or accept negotiation. IAC DON'T NAOHTS and IAC WON'T NAOHTS refuse it or return to the unnegotiated default.

In subnegotiation, the sender uses DS, code 1, and the receiver uses DR, code 0. The accompanying values state which party should handle tab stops and may identify stop positions. Values from 1 through 250 are column numbers measured from the left side of the page or screen.
sections.plainLanguage: The two parties first agree to negotiate. Then the sender or receiver can name tab-stop columns and indicate who should handle them.

sections.title: Value Meanings and Selection Rules
sections.content:
A value of 0 means the sender proposes to handle tab stops alone. Values 1 through 250 ask the other party to handle them using the listed columns. Values 251 through 254 are not allowed. A value of 255 asks the other party to handle tab stops without specifying how.

If neither party wants to handle tabs, the receiver must do so. If both want to handle them, the sender handles them, taking the receiver's suggestions into account. Either party can disable further negotiation with the appropriate refusal command.
sections.plainLanguage: If both sides want to handle tab stops, the sender does. If neither does, the receiver must. The sender can also provide suggested stop columns.
